newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya orders journalists out as safety measure.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya orders journalists out as safety measure.

text.p: The breakaway Russian republic of Chechnya is ordering journalists out of the region as a security measure, a Chechen official told Itar-Tass news agency on Thursday.
Several journalists have been kidnapped in Chechnya recently, including four Russians on Tuesday and an Italian photographer who is still missing after being seized nearly two weeks ago.
Two other Russian journalists were freed last months after several weeks in captivity.

Tass said Chechnya's Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told Tass and Russian Television, who between them employ the four kidnapped this week, that the move was ordered "in the interests of journalists' security and with the aim of helping the negotiating process".
Tass said the order for journalists to withdraw would be officially announced in the regional capital Grozny on Friday.
Two Russian journalists were released last month after weeks in captivity. The Chechen government has blamed "bandits" seeking ransom for several kidnappings.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told a news conference in Moscow that negotiations were under way to free the latest set of hostages, but warned that the situation in Chechnya could lead to its isolation.
"My position is far from wanting to isolate the region and republic, but we are moving towards this," he said.

In his annual state of the nation speech earlier in the day, President Boris Yeltsin only briefly mentioned what has been one the leading problems of his presidency, cautioning against rushing peace negotiations with Chechnya.

"Talks are continuing. Step by step confidence is being restored. But it is easy to destroy it and for this reason it is dangerous to artificially speed up the negotiating process," Yeltsin said in his address to members of parliament.

These comments contrasted with suggestions by negotiators from both sides last Sunday that Russia and Chechnya might soon sign a formal peace declaration after their almost two-year conflict which ended with Russian retreat last August.
Under the August terms, the two sides agreed to defer for five years a decision on Chechnya's political status, the issue at the root of their conflict.
Chechnya's separatist leaders still demand full independence but Moscow has ruled this out. The risk of further clashes remains, although both sides appear keen to avoid more violence.
"The main thing has been achieved -- peace in the Chechen Republic has been restored. This is an imperative condition for the solution of all acute problems," Yeltsin said.
"The Chechen crisis has taught us a lot. The bloodshed has been stopped with great difficulty. So that wounds could heal, so that emotions could give way to common sense we need time."

Yeltsin has publicly regretted his decision to send troops to Chechnya in December 1994. Tens of thousands of people died in the fighting that followed in the mainly Moslem region in Russia's North Caucasus.
